paragraphs: Children in care in County Durham live with Durham County Council's own foster carers or with independent agencies such as the services shown above. The council says it is rated Outstanding by Ofsted and splits its fostering staff into geographical teams, so carers have a local contact wherever they live in the county. It says there are many children and young people across the county who need loving homes.

Durham's pay page says a carer looking after one child receives just under £30,000 a year, and more for two or more children. Its worked examples include £50,675.40 a year for experienced carers looking after a three-year-old and a seven-year-old. Payments reflect the number, ages and needs of the children and the carer's skills and training, are reviewed every year, and are partly tax-free; there are extra payments for children with disabilities or complex needs and for caring for a child for at least a year.

Support includes the Prepare to Foster course before approval, paediatric first aid and therapeutic training after it, an out-of-hours emergency duty team, and support groups for carers, their own children and the children they foster. The council's Full Circle team of therapeutic workers and clinical psychologists supports children up to 18. Durham has also adopted the Mockingbird programme, in which a hub carer supports a community of six to ten foster families.

The council is part of Foster with North East, a hub shared with eleven other councils in the region and backed by the Department for Education, which takes first enquiries and runs a buddy scheme for new carers. Durham is also a Fostering Friendly employer, giving its own staff who foster flexibility for meetings and time to settle children in.
Speak to the council and two or three of the services listed here, and compare what each offers before you apply.
